description: We are an interdisciplinary team driven by scientific curiosity and innovation. Our interests span astrophysics, space exploration, physics, biology, environmental science, and technology. We bring diverse perspectives together to turn scientific challenges into creative, research-driven solutions. We welcome curious minds, critical thinkers, researchers, and developers eager to explore the unknown and push the boundaries of discovery.
summary: TRACE is an interactive educational project that explores the legacy of NASA's space exploration hardware. Through an interactive atlas, users discover historic missions to the Moon and Mars, learn about the equipment used, understand its scientific purpose, and explore the discoveries that continue to contribute to our understanding of space. TRACE connects mission history, hardware, and scientific discoveries in one accessible experience. Its goal is to show that even when a mission ends or equipment is no longer active, the knowledge gained can continue to inspire future generations.
details:
TRACE is an interactive educational atlas about the legacy of space exploration hardware. It presents selected missions to the Moon and Mars, allowing users to explore mission records, equipment, mission status, scientific contributions, and historical timelines.

Users can switch between the Moon and Mars, select mission markers, search records, and follow the connection between a spacecraft or instrument and the discoveries it enabled. The project includes Apollo 12's ALSEP instruments, Surveyor 3, the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Lunokhod 1, Spirit, Opportunity, and InSight. Voyager 1 is included as a comparison because it is still traveling and is not an abandoned surface artifact.

TRACE was built as a responsive web experience using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Its coordinates are approximate reference points displayed on a schematic visualization, not scientific navigation data or satellite imagery. Mission information is linked to NASA primary-source resources.

The project aims to make space science history accessible and engaging, while showing how scientific knowledge can outlive the hardware that produced it.
